# Revert The Depot-Mutation-Rate Raise

**Decision.** Keep `p_mut_depot = 0.05`. Raise `elitism` from 2 to 3 instead.

**Date.** 2026-07-10 (committed), decided during the P2 modification round on the blind GA in
[[optimization-methods]].

**Rejected alternative.** `p_mut_depot` 0.05 → 0.10, tried first and reverted after it regressed every
large instance.

## The reasoning that led into the mistake

The {{operator-bake-off}} had just established that depot mutation is the dominant operator factor —
every combination using *Random* depot mutation beat every combination using *Swap*. The obvious
follow-up is: if depot exploration is the lever that matters, apply more of it. Doubling the depot
mutation rate was the data-driven guess.

It was wrong, and by a lot:

> "That **regressed every large instance by 12–17%** (berlin best-of-10 1,060,173 → 1,244,639) — at
> 0.10, ~20 of 200 depot genes reassign per child, destroying good assignments faster than selection
> can exploit them."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/output/experiments/blind_ga/tuned/mod_note.md, 2026-07-10

The mechanism is the standard exploration/exploitation failure stated concretely: on a 200-customer
instance, 10% depot mutation reassigns roughly 20 genes per child. Selection cannot consolidate a good
partition faster than mutation dismantles it. **"Which operator matters most" and "how much of that
operator to apply" are different questions, and the answer to the first does not imply a direction
for the second.**

## The value came from a teammate, and the experiment confirmed it

The 0.05 base value was not the user's own tuning — it was suggested by a collaborator on the project
and adopted as a fixed base for the bake-off, where all numeric parameters were pinned so only
operator types varied.

> "Base numeric values are FIXED (friend's tuned winners); only operator TYPES vary."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/mdvrp/include/bakeoff.hpp, 2026-07-10

The interview confirms the attribution: the `p_mut_depot = 0.05` value came from a **teammate**
(interview, 2026-07-28; the collaborator is not named here). The failed raise therefore does double
duty — it is a negative result *and* an independent check that an inherited constant was already
near-optimal.

> "confirming the friend's 0.05 was already near-optimal. We reverted and raised elitism instead: a
> safe, near-neutral change (no regression). Honest takeaway: C19 is already near a local optimum for
> simple parameter tweaks."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/output/plots/findings.md, 2026-07-10

## What shipped instead

`elitism` 2 → 3. Deliberately modest: higher elitism protects the best individuals, which is what the
best-of-10 reporting protocol actually selects on, without disturbing the tuned operator behaviour.
Measured as near-neutral — no regression, no dramatic gain. Choosing a change whose *worst* case is
"nothing happens" is the right move once the aggressive change has already cost a full experiment.

## Why the negative result was kept

It would have been trivial to ship `elitism 2→3` with no mention of the failed attempt. Instead the
README's modifications section is titled "Two modifications (**one negative, kept honest**)", and the
regression has its own figure (`fig9_blindga_modification.png`).

That is the same instinct as [[blind-baseline-comparison]], where the GA is reported *losing* to a
greedy heuristic in the headline table, and [[soft-multiplicative-ban-penalty]], where a metric
artefact is published with its before/after. Across this repo, results that make the work look worse
are the ones given figures. See [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]] and
[[keep-the-superseded-version-in-tree]].

A recorded failed parameter change is also worth more later than a successful one: it marks a
direction already searched, which is exactly what nobody writes down.
